articles.title: Women's Super League: York Valkyrie win 12-0 at Leeds Rhinos to book Grand Final place vs defending champions Wigan Warriors
articles.summary: Tries from Liv Wood, Adaoha Akwiwu, in addition to penalty and conversion from Tara Jane Stanley sees York Valkyrie win Women's Super League semi-final at Leeds Rhinos; Watch Grand Final between Wigan and York live on Sky Sports on Sunday September 27 (5.30pm kick-off)
articles.body:
York will now face defending champions Wigan in the Grand Final at the Brick Community Stadium on Sunday September 27 (5.30pm kick-off), live on Sky Sports.

York, who were beaten 38-16 by Leeds on August 8, and 44-0 by Wigan a week later on August 15, have totally turned fortunes around since, defeating Leeds at home, St Helens away and Wigan at home before sealing semi-final success.

The opening 21 minutes proved scoreless at Headingley in a tight contest, before York's Liv Wood twisted, turned and wrestled over to ground the ball for a try in the 22nd minute. Tara Jane Stanley converted for the full haul.

As the first half drew to a close and with Leeds camped on the York try-line on the verge of a try, a grubber-kick on the last by Leeds' Ruby Walker proved a poor one and allowed Stanley to gather and run clear.

Instead, York were next to add points as Stanley struck a penalty superbly from distance for a lead of 8-0 three minutes from the end of the half.

Eight minutes into the second half, Stanley accelerated forward and forced her way over for York's second try and clear daylight on the scoreboard - but the Video Ref then proved via replays she lost control in the act of scoring to rule it out.

Buoyed by their reprieve, Leeds came back attacking hard at York, but Valkyrie defended superbly to keep their two-score lead intact.

On the hour mark, Leeds' Georgia Elliston powered her way over under the sticks for a try, but again the score was ruled out by the Video Ref, who ruled obstruction.

York then wrapped up victory through Adaoha Akwiwu's try as she burst through off a Stanley short-ball pass for a 12-0 advantage.

With six minutes remaining, Leeds' Ebony Stead appeared to charge over for a try out wide to give Rhinos brief hope, but for a third time on the night the Video Ref ruled out a score, as replays proved Stead had lost control of the ball while going over.

The contest ended on a sour note for York too, with the news Stanley - their standout performer on the night - had failed a Head Injury Assessment (HIA), ruling her out of the Grand Final.

Pryce: Nobody gave us a chance - we've made it against all odds

York Valkyrie head coach Leon Pryce to Sky Sports:

"This is unbelievable. Nobody gave us a chance.

"Everyone had written us off, and last week they were saying it was going to be another Saints vs Leeds game after Saints won here.

"We read the comments and used that as fuel. I don't think we got the respect we deserved, but they've been unbelievable.

"To come to Leeds in a semi-final against a really good squad and keep them to zero just shows.

"It was going to be about grit, toughness and determination.

"Against all odds we've got there and I couldn't be more proud.

"I've been proud of them all season, but the last four or five weeks we've really turned a corner and we don't want the season to end."

Wigan trio make up shortlist for 2026 Woman of Steel

Wigan Warriors will dominate the 2026 Woman of Steel awards, with three players from the reigning Women's Super League champions shortlisted for the competition's most prestigious individual honour.

Jenna Foubister , Eva Hunter and Megan Williams have all been named on the three-player shortlist ahead of Rugby League Awards Night in Manchester, which will take place on the evening of Tuesday September 29.

Foubister's nomination comes after another influential season at the heart of Wigan's attack in 2026. The 19-year-old half-back contributed a return of nine tries in 18 appearances across all competitions and has continued to establish herself as one of the leading playmakers in the women's game. Foubister also produced a Player of the Match performance in the Women's Challenge Cup Final at Wembley Stadium, creating two tries and providing three line-break assists as the Warriors lifted the trophy for a second time.

Reigning Woman of Steel Hunter has enjoyed another prolific campaign under Denis Betts, crossing for 23 tries in all competitions. The dynamic second-rower has continued to showcase her devastating pace, powerful ball-carrying and defensive intensity throughout the season, while also writing her name into the history books by becoming the first woman to score four tries in a Challenge Cup Final at Wembley Stadium.

Williams' place on the Woman of Steel shortlist follows a remarkable first two seasons with the Cherry & White, having quickly established herself as one of the competition's most consistent forwards. Since joining the club ahead of the 2025 campaign from St Helens, the England Knights international has become a key figure in Betts' side. The loose forward has scored four tries since the competition split into the Super Four phase, helping Wigan maintain their push for another historic season.

Watch the Women's Super League Grand Final between Wigan Warriors and York Valkyrie live on Sky Sports on Sunday September 27, with kick-off at 5.30pm.

images.caption: Image: York proved the better side defensively and in attack on the day vs Leeds

articles.title: Super League play-off eliminator: Wakefield Trinity v Leigh Leopards kicks off 2026 play-offs
articles.summary: From unfancied to challenging at the top - Wakefield and Leigh meet in a Super League play-off on Friday, aiming to continue their respective trajectories.
articles.body:
Not so long ago, this was a fixture between two of Super League's unfancied teams.

Whether it was Wakefield battling at the bottom of the table, or Leigh fighting to even remain in Super League, these two sides rarely basked in optimism or bigger-picture successes on the field.

That has changed in recent times, however.

Trinity host Leigh in the first of this season's Super League play-off fixtures as they kick off the eliminator phase of the competition on Friday.

Neither have reached a Super League Grand Final - will 2026 be the year?

Wakefield win at Leigh to confirm home play-off

For Daryl Powell, his Wakefield side have done much to turn around their fortunes during his tenure.

His arrival at the club, which coincided with investment from owner Matt Ellis, started the upturn as Trinity won the Championship League Leaders' Shield in 2024 and returned to Super League for the 2025 season.

On their return to the top flight, the club offered no indication that they were happy to make up the numbers and they clinched a top-six place and a play-off spot at the first time of asking.

They fell short 12 months ago but with some smart recruitment, Wakefield have impressed this season. They battled with top spot for much of the campaign before eventually finishing fourth - their highest-ever Super League finish.

"I'm really proud of the whole organisation," Powell told BBC Radio Leeds.

"It comes from a lot of different people, from what we do with recruitment with Millsy [director of rugby Ste Mills] to the coaching team, which is like a band of brothers almost.

"The playing group have been outstanding."

Ultimately, Wakefield fell short of what would have been an outstanding League Leaders' Shield triumph, losing three of their final six games - including defeats by Leeds and Wigan.

As for where his side goes from here, Powell believes a spot in the Grand Final must be the aim.

"For me to be supporting all that and driving what we do as a culture, to give us a chance to be a top-four club, we want to be a consistent top-four club," he added.

"But then it's about getting [to the] play-offs, winning games in play-offs and having a crack at the Grand Final.

"I've really enjoyed my time here. It's an awesome club and I think it's going to be a special club for years to come."

Wakefield are not the only club with investment and momentum heading into the post-season and Friday's opponents have already broken into the upper echelons of Super League.

Since their return to the top flight in 2023, Leigh have rebranded as the Leopards and competed in the play-offs in each campaign since, in addition to winning the Challenge Cup.

Leopards boss Adrian Lam knows the tie is so important because of how close they have previously come to a spot in the Grand Final.

"[We have] finished fifth, fourth, third and then back to fifth again this season," he told BBC Radio Manchester.

"Two years in a row, people forget that we were 80 minutes away from Old Trafford and both at the hands of Wigan who ended up being in that Grand Final.

"Maybe if we had a different path then things might have been different, but we've always been striving to be better to find a different path and maybe get to Old Trafford."

Despite kicking off their season with victory against Leeds, Leigh lost eight out of the following 16 games in all competitions, before winning nine of 12 games to close out the regular campaign.

They were, however, defeated at home by Wakefield last week - but Lam is unmoved about such a statistic.

"Maybe this is the year but I've been grateful of the group and everyone's worked really hard," he added.

"We weren't great last week but that's OK, it's 'where there's life, there's hope' so here we go."

From the verge of quitting to Dream Team glory

Leigh's Umyla Hanley has just been named in his second successive Super League Dream Team - no mean feat given he has played just 17 games this season - and looks set to be part of England boss Brian McDermott's plans before the Rugby League World Cup, which starts in October.

Yet the 24-year-old's successes in the Leigh shirt, particularly since moving to centre, may never have happened at all and he may have been destined for a job as a builder having seen his opportunities with Wigan fizzle out.

"I grew up in Wigan, I'm from Wigan, came to the first team after the academy and just didn't really get that much game time and didn't really know how to handle it as a young lad," he told BBC Radio Manchester.

"I just kind of fell out of love with the game of rugby. I was going to hang it up and just work on site with my mates and have a laugh. But then Lammy gave me a call and he got me down to Leigh and the rest is history."

As for what inspired him not to quit rugby league, Hanley points to the camaraderie in the Leigh camp.

"It's when you're in the changing rooms with the lads after the game, before the game, even in training," he continued.

"Those kind of moments, you can't buy, and then when you perform well on the pitch as well it's just just a big bonus."

In only his second season in Super League, Wakefield's Caleb Hamlin-Uele has broken into the Dream Team ranks himself.

Even more impressive is that in that time he has made only 38 Super League appearances in total, but he bats away any suggestion that his excellent form is all his own doing.

"It's a testament to how hard I've worked and how hard everyone else behind me has worked, because it's not just me," he said.

"There's so many people that are behind closed doors that don't really get any limelight, but I'm grateful to have them all in my corner."

Hamlin-Uele, who missed last season's play-offs through injury, also missed last week's win at Leigh, but hopes he play his part on Friday.

"There's nothing more I want to do than just be with my brothers on that field, just trying to get us to Old Trafford," he said.

articles.title: Red Roses: Jess Breach, Alex Matthews return for England Women vs Canada as John Mitchell rings changes
articles.summary: John Mitchell's England Red Roses face Canada in first of three Tests on Saturday, playing side they beat at Twickenham to win 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup; Red Roses face Canada in WXV Global Series on Saturday in Exeter, and then away on Friday October 16 and Friday October 23
articles.body:
Breach and Matthews, both of whom played major roles in 2025's Women's Rugby World Cup glory - as England beat Canada in the final - come into the side on the right wing and at No 8 respectively.

Mitchell's side face Canada in Tests on Saturday in Exeter, Friday October 16 in Toronto, and Friday October 23 in Ottawa. They also face New Zealand on Saturday September 26 at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Hooker Bryony Field scored on her international debut last weekend in the dominant win over Australia and earns a maiden start in an all-changed front row featuring Hannah Botterman and Maud Muir. Morwenna Talling is also back among the starting contingent from the second row.

Lucy Packer - another try scorer against the Wallaroos - is named at scrum-half with fly-half Zoe Harrison outside her. Helena Rowland is reinstated to the midfield alongside captain Meg Jones.

Three Exeter Chiefs players - Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Maddie Feaunati and Flo Robinson - are in the squad as the Red Roses prepare to play at their club stadium, Sandy Park, for the first time since September 2023.

"This is the first Test of an exciting three-Test series between the No 1 and No 3 teams in the world," head coach Mitchell said.

"You need rivalries in our sport and our rivalry with Canada is one that has evolved to a great level. They are a well-coached team who will bring a different challenge to the one Australia presented. We will be expected to raise our standards."

England's squad contains 974 Test caps, while 14 players in the matchday 23 were involved in the World Cup final triumph over Canada at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Red Roses: 15 Ellie Kildunne, 14 Jess Breach, 13 Megan Jones (c), 12 Helena Rowland, 11 Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, 10 Zoe Harrison, 9 Lucy Packer; 1 Hannah Botterman, 2 Bryony Field, 3 Maud Muir, 4 Morwenna Talling, 5 Lilli Ives Campion, 6 Abi Burton, 7 Sadia Kabeya, 8 Alex Matthews.

Replacements: 16 May Campbell, 17 Mackenzie Carson, 18 Sarah Bern, 19 Delaney Burns, 20 Maddie Feaunati, 21 Marlie Packer, 22 Flo Robinson, 23 Holly Aitchison.

articles.title: Joe Marchant sets sights on England comeback after Sale arrival
articles.summary: Joe Marchant is determined to convince England head coach Steve Borthwick of his Test credentials and convert his famous father-in-law to Sale's cause.
articles.body:
"I've had a couple of near slip-ups, which I didn't tell any of the lads, where I'm just saying the things you'd say there," he says of training with his new Sale team-mates after three years at Paris-based Stade Francais.

"You can feel the words coming out wrong.

"For a high ball in France, you'd say 'j'ai', meaning 'I have'.

"So I have had to style that out and turn it into 'Joe's'."

Marchant's immersion in French life was swift and total.

He won the most recent of his 26 England caps in the third-place play-off win over Argentina at the 2023 Rugby World Cup. He had been head coach Steve Borthwick's first-choice outside centre throughout the tournament, starting every match bar the pool-stage thrashing of Chile.

But, as England took a lap of honour at Stade de France, Marchant was straight into Top 14 life and the Test exile that accompanies it.

"It was a bit of a strange one, everyone was going home and for me Paris was my new home," the 30-year-old remembers.

"We finished on the Saturday with the boys [England] and I had the team photo with Stade on the Tuesday, so it was just an on-to-the-next mentality."

Alongside the language, Marchant picked up plenty on the pitch during his stint in France. He feels he is a more assertive and communicative player than the one that left Harlequins. The Top 14 pushed him physically as well.

"It is such an intense league," he says. "Every weekend, there's someone who is at least 150kg who always sits out of a five man line-out, and you just have to get ready for that coming every week."

What's coming next in England is less predictable.

Borthwick has asked Marchant, like fellow Sale new boy Courtney Lawes, to prove himself in the Prem before any return to the Test fold.

"Steve and I have had a couple of chats here and there. Nothing crazy, but just a couple of chats," says Marchant.

"That was the main message. Get back on the field and play and see where we go.

"I want to play for England, that's what I want to do. I'm proud to have played for England and I don't want it to be my last time at that World Cup. I want to play again."

Marchant well knows how precious and precarious a Test career can be.

His decision to move to Stade Francais was partly motivated by a chat with Borthwick's predecessor Eddie Jones.

"There were those conversations just before the Autumn Internationals [in 2022] that I wasn't fitting the mould and I wasn't going to play in the World Cup," says Marchant.

"The Stade offer was a good offer that, on the back of the England stuff, seemed like the right thing to do.

"Then three weeks later, Eddie wasn't with England any more."

In the aftermath of Twickenham jeers and a Springbok defeat, Jones had been sacked. Marchant may have signed with Stade for the following season, but Borthwick was still a fan.

"Steve brought me in and we had a really honest chat about who I am as a player, my decision to go abroad and who I am as a person," says Marchant, of his 2023 return to the England fold.

"They were all really positive. From that, we just got pretty aligned. He knew what he wanted from me and how to get it. For me, I just felt like it was really good clarity on what I need to do to get into that England shirt."

Marchant, a rangy runner with an excellent nose for an angle or support line and an impressive aerial game, is an intriguing addition to England's existing midfield options.

Sale, with ambitions to play more expansively after significant squad investment, will hope to provide a platform for both Marchant and Lawes to make their cases a year out from the next Rugby World Cup.

They begin at home to Bristol on Saturday, 26 September. The match away to Newcastle Red Bulls also looms large in Marchant's domestic calendar.

His wife Hollie is the daughter of former Newcastle and England football striker Alan Shearer.

"Yeah, maybe," says Marchant about whether his father-in-law will be down at the Corpacq Stadium to watch him.

"I think the Newcastle game in October will probably be more likely. It's a bit closer to Newcastle.

"Hopefully he's supporting Sale. If he's not, that's not really 'play on'."

Converting Shearer, convincing Borthwick, continuing a Test career - there is plenty to play for for Marchant this season.

Image caption, Marchant was the starting 13 in all of England's knockout games at the 2023 Rugby World Cup
Image caption, Stade Francais twice reached the post-season play-offs in Marchant's three seasons in Paris

articles.title: England v Canada: Bryony Field to make first Red Roses start
articles.summary: Hooker Bryony Field will make her first start for England as the Red Roses take on Canada, who they beat in last year's World Cup final, in the WXV Global Series
articles.body:
Hooker Bryony Field will make her first start for England as the Red Roses take on Canada, who they beat in last year's World Cup final, in the WXV Global Series at Exeter's Sandy Park on Saturday.

Field, who scored a debut try off the bench in the 48-15 win over Australia last weekend, is a product of Huddersfield RFC and was cheered on by a clutch of young girls from the club in the win over the Wallaroos in Salford.

England have a number of absences at hooker with Amy Cokayne injured, Connie Powell recovering from surgery and Lark Atkin-Davies having recently become a mother.

Field starts alongside Maud Muir and Hannah Botterman, who were also part of the replacement front row which helped turn last weekend's game the hosts' way.

There is a new-look half-back combination with Lucy Packer and Zoe Harrison at scrum-half and fly-half respectively, while Jess Breach and Alex Matthews return from injury.

In total, 14 of the squad were also in the matchday 23 for their landmark world-title win the last time the teams met.

"You need rivalries in our sport and our rivalry with Canada is one that has evolved to a great level," said England head coach John Mitchell.

"They are a well-coached team who will bring a different challenge to the one Australia presented. We will be expected to raise our standards."

England have won 34 of their 38 meetings with Canada, including their last 14 in a row. Canada's last victory in the fixture was a 52-17 win in Salt Lake City back in 2016.

After taking on Canada, England will play New Zealand, their closest challengers in the world rankings, at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium on Saturday, 26 September.

Their WXV Global Series campaign then continues on the other side of the Atlantic in October with Tests against Canada in Toronto and Ottawa and a meeting with the United States in New Jersey.

England: Kildunne; Breach, Jones, Rowland, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, Packer; Botterman, Field, Muir, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Kabeya, Matthews

Replacements : Campbell, Carson, Bern, Burns, Feaunati, Packer, Robinson, Aitchison

Live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app

images.caption: Image caption, Field went over at the back of a driven maul to score her first Test try against Australia last weekend

articles.title: Scotland Women: Ainsworth makes first start as Bonar returns on bench
articles.summary: Scrum-half Ceitidh Ainsworth will make her first start for Scotland Women, while lock Sarah Bonar makes the match-day squad for the first time since the 2025 Rugby World Cup, for Saturday's visit by New Zealand.
articles.body:
Ceitidh Ainsworth will make her first start for Scotland Women, while experienced lock Sarah Bonar makes the match-day squad for the first time since the 2025 Rugby World Cup, for Saturday's visit by New Zealand.

Having made her debut off the bench in last weekend's 64-26 defeat by Canada, Glasgow Warriors' Ainsworth replaces clubmate Rhea Clarke at scrum-half in one of four changes made by interim head coach Dave Butcher for the WXV Series match at Hive Stadium.

Glasgow lock Holland Bogan returns to the matchday squad to make her second start for Scotland.

Sale Sharks' Eva Donaldson also comes into the starting line-up on the openside flank against the Black Ferns and, in the front row, Glasgow's Anne Young will start at loosehead prop.

Harlequins' Bonar is set to earn her 52nd cap from the bench as she returns from injury.

Clarke drops to the bench along with Sale prop Leah Bartlett, while Bristol Bears second row Hollie Cunningham and Glasgow forward Becky Boyd drop out the match-day squad.

articles.title: Campbell Ridl: Exeter winger set to miss season with knee injury
articles.summary: Exeter winger Campbell Ridl is set to miss much of the season after suffering a knee ligament injury.
articles.body:
Exeter winger Campbell Ridl is set to miss much of the season after suffering a knee ligament injury.

Ridl had been one of the breakout stars of last season, scoring 17 tries in 24 games including one in Exeter's Prem final loss to Northampton Saints at Twickenham.

The 21-year-old, an England Under-20 player, was hurt in Exeter's opening pre-season game when they lost to Welsh side Scarlets earlier this month.

It is the latest injury blow for Exeter, who will be without Italy lock Andrea Zambonin until November with a shoulder problem.

"It's a pretty significant knee injury, it's ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) with bits and pieces, which looks like cartilage damage as well," Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter told BBC Sport.

"You're talking majority of the season. Good ones can recover pretty quickly and a really fast rehab can be around six months, and then you talk anything up to the nine-month period and beyond if there's more complications.

"I don't think it's going to be a six-month one because of the other bits that have also been damaged in the knee, so unfortunately for Campbell it's going to be relatively long-term this season."

Meet 'the Ostrich' - Exeter's flying wing from out of Africa

Exeter hat-trick winger Ridl a 'huge talent'

Baxter urges Ridl to build on impressive season

Ridl was hurt as he slowed down to get a pass away in Exeter's opening pre-season game, rather than being injured in contact. He tried to play on but was forced to come off the field a few minutes after being hurt.

It is a blow for a player who was seen as one of the brightest prospects in English rugby last season.

He scored back-to-back hat-tricks in Prem Rugby Cup games in February and notched six tries in six Prem games between mid-March and mid-May.

"There's never a good time to have a serious injury," added Baxter.

"But having it at a time when he's played his first decent amount of adult rugby in a proper, tough, long season... now he's got that opportunity to really work on his physical development because obviously the challenges of being ready to play games every weekend are not going to be there.

"There's a good deal of physical development he'll be able to do while he's recovering from injury.

"He's also at university and deep in studies, so you've got to try to look at the positives of these things.

"If it gives him a period of really good development, getting on top of university studies, getting things really in line for next season then you've got to try and look at this as part of the development process he's going to go through over the next five or six years of his career."

images.caption: Image caption, Campbell Ridl scored Exeter's opening try in their Prem Rugby final loss to Northampton at Twickenham in June

articles.title: Fin Smith sets England autumn form ultimatum
articles.summary: England fly-half Fin Smith says an under-par autumn would trigger fundamental questions about the team's direction.
articles.body:
England fly-half Fin Smith says an under-par autumn should trigger fundamental questions about the team's direction.

The 24-year-old was asked by Rugby Union Weekly about the state of the team after a miserable Six Nations and a summer campaign that featured a 45-21 defeat by world champions South Africa, a 73-8 thrashing of Fiji and a narrow 31-24 win over Argentina.

"I am not going to sit here and say 'we are building' because that is what you will get every time.

"We will honestly find out in the autumn. If we have a pretty ropey autumn, on the back of building some momentum over the summer, I think we will need to have a pretty hard look at ourselves."

England will play Australia, Japan and New Zealand on successive weekends in November, before a play-off against a southern hemisphere opponent in the finale of the new Nations Championship competition.

"Playing New Zealand at Allianz Stadium will be a great way to test ourselves," said Smith.

"I think on our day, in front of a big crowd and when we are up for it, we can beat anyone. The last time New Zealand came we had a great result."

England beat the All Blacks 33-19 last November in arguably the high point of head coach Steve Borthwick's near four-year spell in charge.

However the team's form has tailed off in 2026, with only three wins in eight Tests. A chastening 42-21 defeat at home by Ireland and a first-ever loss to Italy were among the low points.

Smith, who has started the past five Tests to establish himself as first-choice stand-off ahead of George Ford and Marcus Smith, says he is getting aligned with the demands of Test rugby and Borthwick's gameplan.

"I have been given a fair bit of licence to put my footprint on the attack and lead a lot of meetings about how I want us to play," he said.

"England are probably set up in a slightly different way. Northampton would probably be slightly more attacking and set up with maybe a slightly lighter-weight forward pack that might be suited to the style of play there.

"England is a little bit more set-piece and arm wrestle and tactical, so I have to adapt my game to suit that as well.

"But most of the time I am just going out there to just play what I see."

Marchant set on England comeback after Sale arrival

Rugby Union Weekly: Fin Smith, LRZ, JVP & more!

Dowson admits ambition to step up to Test role

Smith's Northampton boss Phil Dowson has said he has aspirations to eventually coach internationally, having racked up four impressive seasons in charge at Franklin's Gardens.

As director of rugby, the 44-year-old has led Saints to two Prem titles and the 2025 Champions Cup final.

That success has shown in England's selections. Northampton provided six players – more than any other club - to England's Nations Championship squad this summer.

"Fundamentally, we are having a great time at Northampton," Dowson said of himself and head coach Sam Vesty.

"From a personal point of view, at some point, we'd like to coach international rugby because it is different.

"There's no timeline on that. That's not just England. It is just the opportunity to go and do something different to test ourselves - either as a team or individually - under different pressure and to have new experiences."

Dowson said there has been no contact from the Rugby Football Union about preparing him for such an opportunity with England.

He prepared a developmental England XV's forwards , external for a fixture against the Barbarians in May 2019, but has not been brought into the fold since.

Vesty, meanwhile, was seconded to be the attack coach for England A's 91-5 rout of Portugal in February 2024. Back in 2017, he also stepped in as skills coach under Eddie Jones for England's summer tour to Argentina.

Image caption, Phil Dowson (right) and Sam Vesty have guided Northampton to two domestic titles and a runners-up finish in the Champions Cup during their time on the staff

articles.title: Ireland WXV: Head coach Scott Bemand says series represents 'a turning of the page'
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says the forthcoming WXV series represents an opportunity to start bringing on new talent with the 2029 World Cup in mind.
articles.body:
Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says the upcoming WXV Global Series represents the beginning of a new cycle for his squad leading into the next Women's Rugby World Cup in three years' time.

The Irish team were edged out by France at the quarter-final stage of last year's World Cup and finished third in the 2026 Six Nations, winning all three of their home matches.

Ireland open their WXV Global Series campaign against the United States at Dublin's Tallaght Stadium on Sunday (13:45 BST).

Bemand's side then face Japan in a double-header in Galway and Cork on 27 September and 3 October - the first of which is a WXV game - before WXV games against South Africa in Cape Town on 24 and 31 October.

"We're at the start of a World Cup cycle now. The Six Nations, we wanted to keep the momentum from the World Cup going and this is the sort of turning of the page," Bemand told reporters at the Dublin training base.

"Looking three years ahead, what do we need to get under our belts before then?

"We need to develop our depth and see who is coming through. Three years' time there is the potential of something like 28 caps to play for so if you're a new cap coming in now and you go to the World Cup you have the potential of 25-plus caps.

"So we're starting to see talent and understand what talent we need to bring through and this represents the first chance to do that."

Second row Sam Monaghan has been ruled out of the forthcoming fixtures with an Achilles injury but Bemand says her absence and that of other injured players opens a door for others to show what they can do.

"It creates the next opportunity for the leader that's already in the group and the next second row to come through," he said.

"We've been developing depth quietly in the background, those girls get an opportunity to train with us and put their hand up for selection and hopefully we'll see a few of those in this series.

"We're starting to build strength on our shores and we have three games coming up now in the global series. We want to have the ability to go deeper in tournaments so you need to build experience."

The Ireland head coach believes his side can improve further in terms of results and performances if they continue to work hard.

"We've got the talent now and the capability to play a couple of different ways but a really good brand of rugby," he said.

"It's exciting, it's fast-paced, it's got power, it's got movement, we're going to be able to kick the ball, we're going to be able to field the ball.

"It feels like we are on the cusp of something. It won't just happen because each year teams will take us a bit more seriously and those final per cents are always the hardest per cents to come by - but the harder we try, the better we will get, the luckier we'll get, the bounce of the ball will go the other way.

"The players turn up every day, every week, trying to get better and it's a pleasure to watch and to be a part of."

images.caption: Image caption, Bemand was appointed Ireland head coach in July 2023

articles.title: New Zealand: 'Weird and cool' - Mike Blair relishing All Blacks adventure
articles.summary: Former Scotland scrum-half Mike Blair reveals his excitement after teaming up with Dave Rennie as New Zealand attack coach and the prospect of facing up against his home country.
articles.body:
Foreign coaches are about as rare in All Black rugby as the Maui dolphin and the Kakapo parrot, which makes Mike Blair a unique individual in the Land of the Long White Cloud.

Speaking on the BBC Scotland Rugby Podcast, Blair describes his new life as Dave Rennie's attack coach with the All Blacks, a high-profile and high-pressure job, a unique honour, all the more welcome because Scottish coaches in elite rugby are desperately thin on the ground.

Blair is seven Tests into his time in New Zealand - wins over France, Ireland, Italy and South Africa and three defeats all against the world champions in the murderous series they called Rugby's Greatest Rivalry.

In November, Blair, a former Scotland captain with 85 caps to his name, will return home wearing not the blue of his homeland but the black of his adopted country. Scotland versus New Zealand at Murrayfield will be a trippy occasion, he admits.

"I don't know how it'll feel," he says. "I'll tell you once we're there, but it'll definitely be weird and cool. I'm looking forward to it."

Ainsworth makes first Scotland start as Bonar returns on bench

Fin Smith sets England autumn ultimatum to hit form

WXV series about 'turning the page' for Ireland

Blair is now coaching some of the illustrious backs of their generation - Jordie Barrett, Beauden Barrett, Will Jordan, Damian McKenzie among others. All iconic All Blacks and all, he says, fully aware of the threat Scotland pose these days.

It's not lip service, it's proper respect. "You know, it might have been a different thing if it had been 15 years ago, when I was playing. I've spoken to the guys about Scotland and New Zealand games in recent years and each player I've spoken to said, 'Geez, that was a hell of a game'.

"The respect for Scotland's attacking game is huge. Previously, when I played, there's an interview, and I can't remember who it was [an All Black], but they basically couldn't name any of the Scotland players. Now you speak to Jordie and he's naming everyone in the Scotland backline."

That contest will be seismic, as is Blair's own story. "I went straight from finishing in Japan [he coached alongside Rennie in Kobe for three years] on 14 June to starting the job with New Zealand on 17 June. It's been non-stop from there. Eye-opening. Different. Challenging. And a lot of fun as well."

Blair and Rennie are tight, of course. They worked together when the Kiwi was at Glasgow Warriors and renewed their partnership in Japan. Blair had coached Edinburgh before all of that and left his position early, unsure of what life had in store for him. It's been a wild ride since then.

Rennie is his mentor and his champion. "He's good company. He's got lots of stories. The way he manages is not suffocating. He offers opinion when he feels that it's necessary, but otherwise he trusts you to do a job because he's chosen you for a reason.

"He'd spoken to me in Japan and said he was asked to apply for the New Zealand job. So he'd asked me at that stage, would it be something that I was interested in - and I said, yes.

"I was actually back in Edinburgh and it was the middle of the night when they decided who was going to be the head coach. I woke up at seven in the morning, checked my phone and saw that Rens had got the job.

"And then I didn't hear from him. I'd messaged and said, 'Awesome, well done' and then kind of waited for him to say, 'We'll have to sort your contract out', but there was a day's pause because it was difficult with the time difference. There's a pause and I was like, 'We are going to sort this out…' I was hanging in the balance a little bit."

Clearly, Rennie has had an enormous influence on Blair. "He makes you feel really confident about what you do. Like, I questioned if this would be something I'd be able to add value to. I had those thoughts and Dave knew I had those thoughts. He reassured me.

"He stuck his neck out for me - and he wouldn't have done that if he didn't believe that I'd do a good job. Dave's head's on the line here and he's chosen me to do that job. I trust him as a rugby man and so I've got to trust the fact that he's chosen me."

The landscape is different now, the quality of player he's dealing with is sky high, the rugby IQ through the roof.

"I was apprehensive about the quality of people and that I couldn't afford to make a mistake. In Japan, or even with Edinburgh, I'd say, 'Look, this is the plan. What do you guys think?' And it's like, 'Yeah, cool'. Here it was, 'Why are we doing this? Would it not be better to do that?' It was fantastic, but at the same time, it was like, 'I've got to be on it here, because if I'm not, someone's going to find me out'."

Rennie succeeded Scott Robertson, an unhappy time for the All Blacks, who felt they lost some identity on his watch. Blair's first games as attack coach were wins against France, Ireland and Italy in the summer, then came the head-wreck of four straight Tests against the Springboks, three in South Africa and one in Baltimore in America.

In sensational style, New Zealand won the opener in Johannesburg, a five tries to one win that was breathtaking to watch. The Boks being the Boks won the next three, two of them by narrow margins.

For Blair, though the defeats hurt, there were signs of progression. New Zealand's attack really fired. They won the try count over the four Tests, they had more line breaks and beat more defenders. It was South Africa's suffocating physicality and incredible street smarts that won them the series, but there was something to build on for Blair in his new world.

"The mental and physical burden was pretty high, but I still believe we created a way of playing that the guys are really passionate about," he adds. "We've had seven Test matches and we're finding our way.

"It's pretty tough doing that against the best team in the world, so, it's been cool. We believe that if we played to the best of our ability, then we would have won more than one Test match. There's work for us to do, but they [the Springboks] are certainly not unbeatable."

He has two games against Australia to come and then it's the journey home and that Test at Murrayfield. A welcome, of sorts, awaits him.

Image caption, New Zealand suffered defeat against world champions South Africa

articles.title: Northampton Saints cancel memorial wall project for fans' ashes
articles.summary: The club says there has not been enough demand for the project.
articles.body:
A plan for a memorial wall that would have included the ashes of Northampton Saints rugby fans has been cancelled.

The Saints Memorial Wall was to have been part of a wider development to enhance the fan village at the Prem Rugby side's Franklin's Gardens ground.

However, the club said initial demand "was not sufficient to support the long-term viability of the development".

Supporters who have already paid will receive a refund, Saints said.

"When we launched the Saints Memorial Wall, we did so believing it could provide a meaningful and lasting tribute for supporters and their loved ones at the heart of Franklin's Gardens," said the club's chief executive, Julia Chapman.

"Having carefully reviewed the level of demand we concluded that it was not right for us to proceed with the project.

"This was not a decision we took lightly and we recognise that it will be disappointing for some supporters.

"While that is a source of genuine regret, we hope they will understand the reasons behind our decision," she added.

When the project was announced the club said ashes would be interred for 50 years, with costs ranging from £4,000 to £8,000.

Alternative ways for supporters to "create a lasting legacy" at the ground will be explored, it added.

articles.title: England v Canada: Sophie de Goede still loses sleep over World Cup final loss
articles.summary: Canada captain Sophie de Goede says she still loses sleep over their World Cup final loss to England last year.
articles.body:
It is nearly a year since Canada lost the Women's Rugby World Cup final to England - but time has not been a healer for everyone.

"Four to five nights a week I can't fall asleep because I'm still thinking about the final," says Canada captain Sophie de Goede, who is preparing to take on the world champions this Saturday at Sandy Park in Exeter.

So, is this match revenge for the side ranked third in the world?

Canada head coach Kevin Rouet is keen to play this down: "Revenge is a good brand but they [England] won the final of the World Cup - that was the most important game to win, the next important games will be in the World Cup 2029."

After Canada, England play New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, before two more tests against Canada in Toronto and Ottawa. In recent history, England's women have never faced such tough successive opposition.

Red Roses head coach John Mitchell says the games are an "audition" for the 2029 World Cup.

"You look at the geography that we're going to cover, we're not always going to be in our training base. We're going to be going to different facilities. It's a challenge," he said.

"It's going to be really cool to see how they handle pressure as well. I think the Red Roses are very good around pressure because I think it reveals how much they care".

There continues to be misconceptions around the status of the Canadian women: they are professional athletes but contracts, as with most other nations, do not yet compare to England's women.

The Canadian programme involves a clever strategy of using England's domestic PWR league to develop its players.

There are 25 Canadians in PWR and the current Canada coaching staff includes Kevin Rouet and Alex Austerberry , who both coach Saracens Women, and Nathan Smith from Loughborough Lightning.

"It's not like we're coming in to spy," joked De Goede. "We just don't have the quality league [in Canada]."

Canada are not the only country to do this - PWR is littered with top internationals from across the globe.

Mitchell has told BBC Sport that he and Charlie Hayter, head of women's performance at England Rugby, have lobbied to increase PWR game time for English Qualified Players (EQP) from next season.

Mitchell has frequently pushed his theory that players who can reach 1,000 PWR playing minutes a season "gives them a higher probability" of playing for the Red Roses.

"I haven't enjoyed seeing young English players between 21 and 23 not getting enough minutes," he said.

"I think that number [1,000] is very meaningful."

The RFU confirmed to BBC Sport the current requirements around 13 EQP players on average across matchday squads will remain. However, the lure of signing foreign talent will be dampened by the removal of club injury credit, which helps cover the cost of replacing an injured player.

From the 2027-28 season, only players who sustain an injury while on international duty for one of England's representative teams will be eligible.

Besides this, if any EQP player is captured by another union, they will only be able to hold their EQP status until the end of that season.

images.caption: Image caption, De Goede's Canada side were beaten 33-13 by England in the 2025 World Cup final

articles.title: WXV Global Series: Jemima Adams Verling handed Ireland debut for United States opener
articles.summary: Connacht back row Jemima Adams Verling is handed her senior Ireland debut in Sunday's WXV Global Series opener against the United States in Dublin.
articles.body:
Connacht back row Jemima Adams Verling will make her senior Ireland debut in Sunday's WXV Global Series opener against the United States in Dublin.

Adams Verling will line out at blind-side flanker in the back row alongside captain Erin King at open-side flanker and Women's Six Nations player of the championship Aoife Wafer at number eight.

The 20-year-old's ascension to the senior team comes after she impressed in the U18 Women's Six Nations in 2024 and last year's U21 Women's Six Nations while she has also been impressive for the Clovers in the Celtic Challenge.

She was part of this year's Six Nations squad but did not feature.

Head coach Scott Bemand has named an experienced pack with props Niamh O'Dowd and Linda Djougang and hooker Cliodhna Moloney-MacDonald in the front row.

With Sam Monaghan out injured, Dorothy Wall and Fiona Tuite-O'Sullivan line up in the second row.

In the back three, Stacey Flood starts at full-back with Robyn O'Connor and Vicky Elmes Kinlan on the wings. Right winger O'Connor was one of Ireland's breakout players in this year's Six Nations, scoring two tries.

Aoife Dalton and Eve Higgins start in midfield, while Dannah O'Brien and Emily Lane retain their half-back partnership from the Six Nations.

The forward replacements are Neve Jones, Sadhbh McGrath, Eilis Cahill, Jane Clohessy and Brittany Hogan, who scored five tries in this year's Six Nations, with Aoibheann Reilly, Anna McGann and Niamh Gallagher offering backline cover.

Ireland open their WXV Global Series campaign against the United States at Dublin's Tallaght Stadium (13:45 BST), the first women's rugby Test match at the home of football team Shamrock Rovers.

Bemand's side then face Japan in a double-header in Galway and Cork on 27 September and 3 October - the first of which is a WXV game - before WXV games against South Africa in Cape Town on 24 and 31 October.

articles.title: Women's Super League play-off semi-final: Leeds Rhinos 0-12 York Valkyrie
articles.summary: York Valkyrie book their place in the Grand Final with a superb semi-final win over Leeds Rhinos at AMT Headingley.
articles.body:
Betfred Women's Super League play-off semi-final

York Valkyrie will meet reigning Women's Super League champions Wigan Warriors in the Grand Final after beating Leeds Rhinos at AMT Headingley Stadium.

Leon Pryce's team, who last week ended Wigan's 100 per cent record to book their place in the semi-final, managed tries through forwards Liv Wood and Adaoha Akwiwu in a tight contest.

Leeds had inflicted heavy defeats on their opponents in the two regular season meetings at home, but they went into the match on the back of four straight losses, and their lack of confidence showed as they came up with errors at vital moments.

The only downside for York was that their influential stand-off Tara-Jane Stanley will miss the September 27 meeting with Wigan at the Brick Community Stadium after failing a head injury assessment.

That will be a serious blow for York, who beat Wigan 26-12 last week, and a personal blow for Stanley, whose return from a two-year injury absence had sparked their run of four wins in their past five games.

They were on the front foot for most of the game and deservedly went ahead when pressure on the Rhinos line ended with England prop Liv Wood forcing her way over despite the attentions of three tacklers.

Stanley's kicking game was important in the success, and she added the conversion and kicked a penalty to give her side breathing space at half-time.

Leeds rallied in the second half and, after Stanley had a try disallowed for a knock-on and Megan Pakulis was denied a try by a brilliant Ruby Bruce tackle, the Rhinos seemed to have struck back only for Georgia Elliston's try to be disallowed for obstruction by a team-mate.

Stanley came up with the telling moment, a lovely pass to send Akwiwu over for York's second try, and when Ebony Stead fumbled as she went to touch down, the home side's hopes of a late revival were over.

articles.title: WXV Global Series: Inspired Wales stun South Africa in eight-try demolition
articles.summary: Wales return to winning ways in emphatic fashion with an eight-try victory over South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park.
articles.body:
Tries: Keight, Tuipulotu 2, Lockwood, Davies, K Jones, Neumann, Callender Cons: Bell 5

Tries: Jacobs, Tshiremba, Samboya Cons: Dolf 2

Wales returned to winning ways in emphatic fashion with an eight-try victory over South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park.

The hosts had gone nine Tests without a victory heading into their WXV Global Series opener, with a tight contest predicted against a Springboks side ranked three places above them in the world.

But Sean Lynn's bold selections paid off as Wales attacked with a freedom and intent they have not produced for years.

They were six tries to the good in a dominant first half, with the visitors made to pay for indiscipline.

Tighthead Sisilia Tuipulotu was back to her irrestistible best, scoring in either half, while co-captain Alex Callender returned from injury with a typically impressive player-of-the-match display.

Lynn had told his players to be brave in the build-up, and he was courageous with his team selection after moving scrum-half Keira Bevan to 10.

The gamble paid off as the hosts enjoyed a perfect start under Friday night lights and it was fitting that the recently crowned Welsh Rugby Writers' player of the year Courtney Keight bagged the opening score.

Georgia Evans and Tuipulotu had made the hard yards before the ball was spread wide to Keight on the left wing and she cut inside to go over.

Kelsey Jones' turnover provided the launchpad for the second, with Evans popping a neat ball back inside for Tuipulotu to charge to the line.

South Africa responded with Felicia Jacobs benefiting from a dominant scrum on Wales' five-metre line, but that was to be their only score in a one-sided half.

Former Cardiff City footballer Amy Williams came within metres of scoring after winning the footrace to Lisa Neumann's grubber kick, but Seren Lockwood was first to the breakdown and darted over herself.

It was a double blow for the visitors who had hooker Lindelwa Gwala sent to the sin bin for being offside in the build-up.

Wales took full advantage with Maisie Davies showing her power to score her first international try and secure Wales' bonus point.

The hosts were in dreamland, but had to revert to their usual half-back pairing when Lockwood failed to return from a head injury assessment, with Bevan going back to scrum-half and Lleucu George slotting in at 10.

The enforced changes did little to halt Wales' flow with Freya Bell coming agonisingly close from a five-metre driving lineout, but Jones was there to clean up as she crossed over.

South Africa then went down to 13, with lock Danelle Lochner sent to the sin bin for a high tackle on Kate Williams, a card that would later be upgraded to a 20-minute red.

That paved the way for the pick of Wales' first-half tries. A solid scrum provided the platform for the ball to be worked out wide to Neumann who cruised over from her new full-back position.

It was Wales at their clinical best as they headed down the tunnel 38-5 in front.

As we know in Welsh rugby, things are never that straightforward and a wounded South Africa came out a different team in the second half.

Wales had initially picked up where they left off with Tuipulotu powering through some weak tackling for her second of the night to give Wales a 40-point lead.

But South Africa chipped away, with Maria Tshiremba scoring her third try in just two appearances after latching on to a tricky crossfield kick.

They were soon in again with what was arguably the try of the night. It came from the powerful running of Aphiwe Ngwevu who offloaded to her centre partner Maceala Samboya, who showed a good turn of pace to get to the line.

With Wales' defence creaking, they were in need of a little inspiration and that came from Williams, who not only showed great feet down her wing but incredible strength to keep the ball alive for Callender to score.

Front-row forwards Shanelle Williams and Elan Jones came off the Welsh bench to make their debuts and enjoy something many of their team-mates had not experienced in over a year - a Welsh win.

articles.title: Super League play-off eliminator: Wakefield Trinity 26-16 Leigh Leopards - hosts reach semi-finals for first time
articles.summary: Wakefield Trinity reach the Super League semi-finals for the first time in their history with a dominant win over Leigh Leopards.
articles.body:
Betfred Super League play-off eliminator

Tries: Smoothy, Johnstone, Vagana, Faatili Goals: Jowitt 5

Tries: Armstrong, Lam, Senior Goals: Cook 2

Wakefield Trinity reached their first Super League semi-final with a dominant victory over Leigh Leopards.

Daryl Powell's side will face either Leeds Rhinos or Wigan Warriors next week after a powerful display by their pack and tries from Tyson Smoothy, Tom Johnstone, Isaiah Vagana and Caius Faatili proved too much for Leigh.

The away side seemed to be back in the game as David Armstrong's superb try cut the deficit to six points just before half-time, but Trinity controlled the second half.

Even the dismissal of Wakefield forward Emre Guler for a punch could not alter the outcome, although tries from Lachlan Lam and Innes Senior cut the deficit.

Trinity have reached the Super League play-offs four times but have not progressed to the last four before, with Leigh thwarting them last season, their first back in the top flight following promotion.

This time the result never truly looked in doubt, Max Jowitt easing nerves with an early penalty before Smoothy's 40/20 set up field position from which he darted over from dummy half.

The excellent Wakefield pack kept Leigh on the back foot and it was no surprise when Johnstone produced a brilliant flying finish in the corner for another try, although it took a video review to overturn referee Chris Kendall's on-field decision.

Leigh burst into life in the last few seconds of the first half with a superb team move as Lam and Owen Trout combined to send Armstrong away, but Trinity struck first in the second half as Vagana scythed through Leigh's defence to score.

Leigh's defensive errors were piling up and when Jack Ashworth knocked on Faatili spun his way over the line to seemingly put the game beyond the visitors.

That was called into question when Guler, who was due to join Wakefield in 2027 but arrived in England last week to join the play-off push, lost his temper and thrust his fist into Trout's face.

Lam again swapped passes with Trout to scamper over, and for the first time the Wakefield crowd went a little quiet, but a dangerous tackle by Jack Hughes allowed Jowitt to kick a penalty for his 500th Super League point and make sure of the win.

Leigh finished with a late flourish as Senior ended a lovely passing move with a try but it was no more than a consolation by that point.

Wakefield head coach Daryl Powell told BBC Radio 5 Live:

"We got Emre sent off and it looked like it was going to be a tough challenge, but we had built up a bit of a buffer with how well we started the second half.

"They came after us and threw everything at us. That kick-try looked offside, but our boys have been class and did well to dig us out of that pressure at the end.

"At half-time I thought we had dominated the game like we did last week [against Leigh] but the scoreline didn't reflect it.

"We probably should have nailed a couple more pieces of play, but the players were really calm at half-time and we talked about if we got in good attacking positions and were a little more clinical we felt like we could put the game away.

"We did that until Emre gets a red, but I just don't think it's a red. I don't see why [referee Chris Kendall] is so twitchy on that. He refereed the game well in a tense environment. Jazz [Tevaga] gets dropped on his head and that's way more dangerous."

Leigh head coach Adrian Lam told Sky Sports:

"A couple of soft tries was exactly what we didn't need – the story of the night. We rallied, but the first five or seven minutes of the second half was diabolical.

"It was quite a frustrating watch at times. There were too many mistakes and everything we tried not to do.

"Everything we've not done this year has all come out tonight, for some reason. It's down to execution and individuals in big moments."
